prize_parts.citation: For an oeuvre that remakes the boundaries of lyric, essay and verse narrative in dialogue with antiquity, and gives grief and desire new formal shape.

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged: Anne Carson as sole laureate. What the exchange changed is how I would justify it. The chair asked which works form the credited core. From public knowledge I would name Autobiography of Red (the Geryon material as a modern verse novel), Nox (an elegy for a brother built as an object), and the essay and lyric books around them, including Eros the Bittersweet and The Beauty of the Husband. I would accept a citation limited to the original poetry, verse narrative and essays. The classical translations and versions would count as evidence of the same practice, not as separate credited achievements. The case for her is a recurring method. An inherited or fragmentary source is reworked until its form carries an emotional argument about grief, desire or the distance of the past. That method shows up in several modes over several decades, so I read the range as one project, not as scattered modes. She writes in English, so the text itself reaches me without translation loss. That lowers one uncertainty and does not add merit. On my reading of the will, the 'idealistic direction' is seriousness of purpose and intellectual and emotional depth, not a particular subject or genre. The sustained attention to loss, desire and how ancient texts keep speaking fits that reading. Everything here comes from public knowledge, not fresh reading, and I have not independently verified any source.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is delimitation and demonstrability. The central achievement can be stated, but it is most clearly shown in a small number of titles, and I cannot confirm that the later and more performance-oriented books keep the level of the central works. Nox in particular depends on its physical form, which a text-only reading understates, so the committee should not over-claim what it can assess from the printed text. Canonical standing for the hybrid works is not settled. The influence among poets that I know of is partial evidence and not proof. Cărtărescu's single, statable metaphysical architecture is a real counterweight. If the committee judges that unity of project at large scale matters more than breadth of formal reinvention, or reads the will as favouring epic or visionary ambition, I would regard a move toward B009 as a defensible weighting and not an error. My own difference from that view is a weighting I hold with some uncertainty and cannot fully resolve.

responses.point: Olsson prefers Cărtărescu and keeps Carson as first alternative. He argues that Cărtărescu's project has a more stable centre, while Carson's corpus raises a delimitation problem across translation, scholarship, adaptation and object-book work. He also says that the closeness of the opening support gives no reason to change a literary assessment.
responses.response: I agree that closeness of support is no argument and I do not use it. On delimitation, I would answer by drawing the credit narrowly. The original verse novel, elegy and essays would be credited, and the classical versions would be context. That makes the oeuvre honoured smaller, and I accept that cost. Where I still differ is on the stable centre. I read Carson's centre as a method (a source reworked until its form carries the feeling), and I think a method can be as stable as a cosmology. You called the late-Cărtărescu point a public-knowledge judgment. I should also say that my round-1 file did not claim that his late novels extend the earlier vocabulary. I cannot support that claim from reading, and I do not want it counted as evidence for either side.

responses.point: Mattson prefers Cărtărescu and asks for evidence that his late work extends the earlier vocabulary and does not repeat it. She also says Carson's range of modes makes a single achievement hard to define, and that Wright's small corpus does not yet establish sustained quality.
responses.response: I cannot give you that evidence. My round-1 file did not make the claim about Cărtărescu's late novels, and I have no verified reading of them. That question should stay open for his supporters to test, and I do not want it passed to me as settled. On Carson, I take her point that the centre is harder to name than in a single-architecture oeuvre. I would still name it as the reinvention of the lyric and essay book as a vehicle for elegy and desire, visible across decades. I accept that it is clearest in a handful of works. I agree with her principle for Wright, that form, voice and sustained quality count and the symbolism of a theme does not. I rank Wright fifth, so that principle does not change my configuration.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg prefers Carson but says he would not object if the committee moved to Cărtărescu on epic scale. He asks whether Carson's allusiveness narrows the readership and whether her emotional force reaches beyond specialists.
responses.response: I agree that the case must rest on a body of work and that scale is the live competing consideration. I would not make breadth of readership a test of merit. On the narrower question of access, my judgment from public knowledge is that Nox's elegy reaches a reader without classical training, and the classical apparatus adds to it. That is not verified reception data. I differ from you in not treating scale as the tiebreaker. I weigh formal economy and the force of compressed lyric invention at least as heavily as sustained architecture. If a close reading by colleagues showed that the later Carson books only repeat the early devices, that would move me more than any argument about scale.

responses.point: Carlberg prefers Carson, wants the citation to name the emotional pull and not only the classical apparatus, and asks that the later books be tested before the vote, not assumed to match the early ones.
responses.response: I agree on both points. My citation wording puts grief and desire in the credit and does not name antiquity as the achievement. I share your concern about the later work. I have no verified reading of the recent books, and I would treat that as the main open question in my own case. I would not call it a reason to withdraw support. If a colleague with closer knowledge reported that the recent output is thin, I would weigh that seriously.

responses.point: Sward prefers Carson, would anchor the citation in the written text with Nox's physical form as an extension, and concedes that Cărtărescu's project is the more unified. She calls the difference one of weighting that she cannot fully resolve.
responses.response: I agree with anchoring the citation in the written text. The committee can then say openly that Nox's material form is partly lost in a text-only reading, without making that form the main credit. Like you, I regard unity of project against breadth of reinvention as a weighting that cannot be fully settled by argument. The chair's question is whether a closer reading of the other side's central works would move me. For me it would, if it showed that Cărtărescu's late novels deepen the project and that the translated prose holds up at sentence level. I cannot test that myself.

uncertainties: Whether Carson's later and more performance-oriented books sustain the level of Autobiography of Red and Nox; my knowledge of them is secondhand.
How to draw the citation boundary between original poetry, verse narrative and essays and the translations, versions and object-book work, and how much of the achievement a text-only reading loses.
Whether the hybrid works will hold canonical standing or stay influential mainly among writers; this cannot be settled now for a living author.

For Cărtărescu, the closest alternative, whether translation preserves the density of the Romanian prose and whether the long novels sustain quality; I cannot judge either directly, and this limits any direct comparison.
For Tawada, wordplay across Japanese and German is only partly accessible in translation, and the two-language scope complicates a citation.
Whether unity of a single project should outweigh breadth of formal reinvention; I hold my weighting with some uncertainty.
My assessment rests on public knowledge and not fresh reading, and I do not claim independent verification of any source. Opening support counts are not evidence of literary merit.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile, which records no personal, institutional or collaborative tie to any shortlisted writer. My own work on art, creativity and women's lives, and my Selma Lagerlöf biography, are context and not evidence of preference for or against any candidate. As in round 1, nothing has changed to alter this disclosure.
